title: Two ways to be atomic across services
sub: Two-phase commit locks and waits; a saga commits as it goes and undoes on failure.

frames.caption: Two-phase commit. A coordinator (C) runs one transaction across three databases: orders, inventory and payments.
Phase 1, prepare: C asks every participant whether it can commit. Each writes its changes to its durable log, locks the rows, and votes.
All three vote yes. C writes COMMIT to its own log. That write is the point of no return: the transaction is now committed, whatever crashes next.
Phase 2: C tells everyone to commit. Each participant applies its changes and releases its locks. All-or-nothing across three databases.
Two-phase commit. A coordinator (C) runs one transaction across three databases: orders, inventory and payments.
Phase 1, prepare: C asks every participant whether it can commit. Each writes its changes to its durable log, locks the rows, and votes.
All three vote yes. But before C can send its decision, it crashes.
Now the participants are stuck. Each promised to commit if told to, so none can abort on its own; and none knows whether C decided COMMIT or ABORT before it died. They must hold their locks and wait.

Any other transaction touching those rows waits too. Only when C recovers and reads its log can it finish the protocol. This blocking is 2PC's fundamental weakness; systems like Spanner and CockroachDB avoid it by replicating the coordinator's decision with Paxos or Raft.
A saga: the orchestrator (C) runs the checkout as a sequence of local transactions, each committing immediately in its own service. No locks are held across services.
Step 1: the order service creates the order and commits.
Step 2: inventory reserves the items and commits. Other customers can already see that stock is reserved: intermediate state is visible.
Step 3: the card is declined. The payment step fails.
Committed steps cannot be rolled back, so C runs compensating transactions in reverse order: release the reservation...

... then mark the order failed. Each compensation is a new forward transaction, and must be idempotent, since C may crash and retry it. The system ends consistent, but only eventually, and every step was visible on the way.
